records.title: Three men. One ground test.
records.dek: This was a countdown rehearsal, not a launch. The rocket was unfueled; the spacecraft was not free of danger.
records.detail: Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee prepared to rehearse an Apollo countdown at Launch Complex 34. The plugs-out test was treated as comparatively nonhazardous because the Saturn IB was not fueled. The spacecraft still contained a dense oxygen environment, combustible materials and an escape hatch that could not be opened quickly under pressure.
records.caution: An unfueled launch vehicle did not mean a safe cabin.

image.alt: Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee standing near Launch Complex 34 during training in January 1967.
image.caption: The Apollo 1 crew near Launch Complex 34 during training, January 1967.
image.identity_note: NASA record page confirms the credit and caption. The identifier S67-19766 appears in the record page markup but was not found through the NASA Image API nasa_id search; confirm before publication. Delivered from the Final Vestige media library.

crosswalk.claim: The test was a plugs-out countdown rehearsal with an unfueled Saturn IB.
crosswalk.source: Final Vestige article; not re-checked against the Board text in Sprint 5.

records.title: An atmosphere built for a different risk.
records.dek: One hundred percent oxygen at elevated ground-test pressure greatly increased the fire hazard inside Command Module 012.
records.detail: The 1967 Review Board documented a 100 percent oxygen cabin atmosphere at 16.7 pounds per square inch absolute during the ground test. Combustible materials and potential ignition sources were present. This was not the same pressure regime the spacecraft would use in orbit.
records.caution: Oxygen accelerated combustion; it was not itself the ignition spark.

image.alt: Apollo Command and Service Module 012 hanging from a crane above its adapter during preflight processing, with technicians working around it.
image.caption: Spacecraft 012 during preparations for the Apollo/Saturn 204 mission, January 1967. Processing photograph, not an image of the fire.
image.identity_note: NASA Image API nasa_id S67-15717; center JSC; record date 1967-01-03. Verified 2026-10-30.

crosswalk.claim: The test used a 16.7 psia, 100 percent oxygen atmosphere.
crosswalk.source: Board report: 'The test was conducted with a 16.7 pounds per square inch absolute, 100-percent oxygen atmosphere.'

crosswalk.claim: The test conditions were extremely hazardous.

records.title: Fourteen seconds changed the system.
records.dek: The surviving instrument record describes an extraordinarily rapid pressure-and-fire sequence.
records.detail: The first fire transmission began at approximately 23:31:04.7 GMT. About six seconds later the cabin-pressure sensor showed a clear rise; by approximately 23:31:16 its range was exceeded. The pressure vessel ruptured at least 29 psia around 23:31:19. These timings are approximate marks from the Board account, not a reconstructed second-by-second animation.
records.caution: The timeline reports observed markers. The intervals between them are not interpolated sensor measurements.

image.alt: Astronaut Virgil Grissom stepping through a hatch into an altitude chamber while Roger Chaffee follows and Edward White stands with chamber technicians.
image.caption: The prime crew preparing to enter their spacecraft in the altitude chamber at Kennedy Space Center, 18 October 1966. Training photograph taken months before the fire.
image.identity_note: NASA Image API nasa_id S66-58038; center JSC; record date 1966-10-18. Verified 2026-10-30.

crosswalk.claim: The first verbal fire report began at 23:31:04.7 GMT.
crosswalk.source: Board report, chronology: 'the transmission reporting the fire which began at 23:31:04.7 GMT (6:31:04.7 p.m. EST)'.

crosswalk.claim: The first pressure increase was recorded about 6 seconds after the report.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Cabin Pressure Rise: 'about 6 seconds after the crew first reported the fire'. The NASA web text prints the clock time as 23:21:11, an apparent typographical error for 23:31:11; the interval is unaffected.

crosswalk.claim: Pressure exceeded the transducer range (17 psia cabin) by 23:31:16 GMT.
The cabin ruptured at about 23:31:19 GMT at a pressure of at least 29 psia.
crosswalk.source: Board report: 'ruptured at a time of about 23:31:19 GMT and at a pressure of at least 29 psia'; another passage gives 23:31:19.4.
The Board says the first stage ended 'approximately 15 seconds after the verbal report'; its own stamps (04.7 to 19.4) give 14.7 s. Title unchanged pending editorial decision.

records.title: The hatch opened inward.
records.dek: A seal intended to help contain pressure became an obstacle when pressure rose during the fire.
records.detail: The Block I command module used an inward-opening pressure hatch. The Review Board found that pressure relief could not keep up with the fire-driven pressure rise, so the hatch could not be opened before the pressure vessel ruptured. Ed White was responsible for opening the hatch; investigators observed movement consistent with an attempt to begin the procedure.
records.caution: The hatch was one of several interacting hazards, not a standalone explanation of the fire.

image.alt: Display cases in a dimly lit museum gallery holding the sections of the three-part Apollo 1 hatch under the heading 'Portals into the Unknown'.
image.caption: The three-part hatch that was in place on the Apollo 1 spacecraft, displayed in the 2017 tribute at Kennedy Space Center's Apollo/Saturn V Center. A museum display photographed 24 January 2017.
image.identity_note: NASA Image API nasa_id KSC-20170124-PH_KLS01_0129 (record page is the NASA Image Library detail page; a nasa.gov image-detail page was not found for this asset); NASA description: 'The three-part hatch that was in place on the Apollo 1 spacecraft is shown in a tribute'. Replaces KSC-20170124-PH_KLS01_0164 used in the prototype, which shows a spacecraft mockup, not the hatch. Verified 2026-10-30.

crosswalk.claim: Due to internal pressure the inner hatch could not be opened before rupture.
crosswalk.source: Board Finding 4: 'Due to internal pressure, the Command Module inner hatch could not be opened prior to rupture of the Command Module.'

crosswalk.claim: The Block I hatch opened inward.
crosswalk.source: Not located in the Board report landing-page text; source from NASA history or exhibit text before publication.

records.title: The spark was never conclusively identified.
records.dek: Investigators found probable evidence of electrical arcing, but the final ignition source remained unproven.
records.detail: The Apollo 204 Review Board identified an electrical arc in or near the probable origin area as the most likely initiator. Fire damage destroyed crucial physical evidence; it did not conclusively establish one wire or arc as the ignition source. The Board nevertheless documented vulnerable wiring, combustible materials, the hazardous oxygen environment and inadequate egress provisions.
records.caution: Probable is not proven. This experience deliberately keeps the uncertainty visible.

image.alt: Close view of the charred interior of Apollo Command Module 012 at Pad 34 showing heavy heat and fire damage.
image.caption: Interior of Command Module 012 at Pad 34, photographed 28 January 1967, the day after the fire. No people are shown.
image.identity_note: NASA Image API nasa_id S67-21294; center JSC; record date 1967-01-28. Verified 2026-10-30.

crosswalk.claim: The Board's search for the specific initiator was unsuccessful.
crosswalk.source: Board report: 'A great deal of effort has been expended in an attempt to find this specific initiator. Although unsuccessful in this search...'

crosswalk.claim: An electrical arc was the most likely initiator.
crosswalk.source: Board text found: arcing considered as a possible cause of transients; electrostatic discharge, spontaneous combustion, mechanical heat and impact heat 'eliminated as reasonable possibilities'. The exact 'most probable' arc sentence was not located in the extracted text; confirm wording.

records.title: Inward became outward.
records.dek: The redesigned Block II hatch could be opened outward quickly; the safety overhaul extended far beyond the hatch.
records.detail: NASA replaced the complex inward-opening hatch with an outward-opening, quick-release assembly. It also changed materials, wiring protection, rescue preparation and safety review. The Apollo investigation article notes 102 deliberate ignition tests of Command Module boilerplate 1224 from December 1967 through February 1968—an example of testing how fire would actually spread rather than assuming it could always be prevented.
records.caution: The improvements were part of a broad redesign; Apollo 1 did not create every safety innovation from nothing.

image.alt: A lit museum display case holding a hatch, with on-image text stating the Block I hatch was designed to open in 90 seconds and the Block II hatch in 5 seconds.
image.caption: The redesigned hatch in the 2017 Apollo 1 tribute at Kennedy Space Center. The exhibit text states the Block I hatch was designed to open in 90 seconds and the Block II in 5. A museum display photographed 24 January 2017.
image.identity_note: NASA Image API nasa_id KSC-20170124-PH_KLS01_0090; NASA description: 'A redesigned hatch for an Apollo spacecraft is shown inside the new tribute'. Verified 2026-10-30.

crosswalk.claim: NASA redesigned the hatch to open outward quickly.
crosswalk.source: Exhibit text in NASA image KSC-20170124-PH_KLS01_0090 (Block II designed to open in 5 seconds); outward direction not located in the Board landing-page text.

crosswalk.claim: 102 deliberate ignition tests of boilerplate 1224, Dec 1967 to Feb 1968.
crosswalk.source: Final Vestige article; not re-checked in Sprint 5.

chronology.title: The recorded markers
chronology.origin_label: First verbal fire report began 23:31:04.7 GMT
chronology.unit: seconds after the first verbal fire report
chronology.notice: Only these four markers are documented in the Board account. The spaces between them are not sensor measurements and nothing is interpolated.

markers.label: First verbal report of fire
markers.note: The crew gave the first verbal indication of an emergency.

markers.label: First indication of a cabin pressure increase
markers.note: About 6 seconds after the report, per the Board account.

markers.label: Pressure exceeded the sensors' range
markers.note: The cabin transducer range was 17 psia; the battery compartment transducer range was 21 psia.

markers.label: Command Module pressure vessel ruptured
markers.note: At a pressure of at least 29 psia. The Board gives both 'about 23:31:19' and 23:31:19.4.
